headline: Legal education, the right to practice and the work of challenging exclusion
summary: Black lawyers built schools and professional networks, practiced privately, joined government legal offices and challenged exclusion in court. These records separate a degree and bar admission from paid work, promotion and judicial appointment.
coverageNote: Ten selected episodes across legal education, professional organizing, private practice, civil-rights litigation and public service. Named workplaces include Howard, the Interior Department, New York City’s Law Department, LDF and the Southern District of New York; they do not establish access at every firm or court.
question: Which bar, firm, court or legal department record establishes Black access to the work you do?

events.title: John Mercer Langston leads a new route into law
events.people: John Mercer Langston and Howard's first law students
events.decisionMaker: Howard University opened its law department under Langston in January 1869.
events.barrier: Howard's account describes a need for lawyers to protect Black Americans' rights after emancipation.
events.change: Six students initially attended evening classes in instructors' homes and offices.
events.outcome: Ten students graduated in February 1871; Howard records that eight entered District of Columbia practice the next day.
events.limit: These are the institution's reported early outcomes, not evidence of equal access to every legal employer.

source.title: Howard University School of Law · Our History
source.locator: History paragraphs covering January 1869, February 1871 and Charlotte E. Ray in 1872
source.supports: Howard’s opening, Langston’s leadership and the first graduates’ reported entry into practice.

events.title: Charlotte E. Ray earns a degree and admission to practice
events.decisionMaker: Howard awarded her degree; she was admitted to the District of Columbia bar.
events.barrier: Racial and gender barriers continued after the credential.
events.change: She earned her Howard law degree and entered District of Columbia practice in 1872.
events.outcome: She opened a law office, but the District’s Attorney General records that she could not obtain enough business to sustain it.
events.limit: Her admission opened a legal right to practice; it did not ensure clients or a durable livelihood.

source.title: District of Columbia OAG · Charlotte E. Ray
source.locator: February 26, 2019; Charlotte E. Ray biography, degree and private-practice paragraph
source.supports: Her 1872 credential, District practice and business closure.

events.title: Black lawyers establish their own national professional network
events.people: George H. Woodson, Gertrude E. Rush and fellow founders
events.decisionMaker: Twelve founders incorporated the National Bar Association in Des Moines; Woodson became its first president.
events.barrier: Some founders had been denied American Bar Association membership.
events.change: They built a national association for professional cooperation and the defense of civil rights.
events.outcome: The association’s early agenda included exclusion of Black lawyers from law libraries and efforts to extend legal services.
events.limit: Association membership did not confer a law license or guarantee employment. Its founding is a professional-organizing record, not evidence about every bar or firm.

source.title: National Bar Association · History
source.locator: Timeline: 1925 incorporation and 1930 library access; founders and past presidents lists
source.supports: The incorporation date, founders, Woodson’s presidency and early access concerns.

events.title: Sadie Alexander enters the Pennsylvania bar and a legal practice
events.people: Sadie Tanner Mossell Alexander and Raymond Pace Alexander
events.decisionMaker: Penn awarded her law degree; Pennsylvania admitted her to the bar; she joined Raymond Alexander's practice.
events.barrier: Despite an earlier economics doctorate, she had struggled to find work in Philadelphia.
events.change: She became Penn Law's first Black woman graduate and, according to Penn Archives, Pennsylvania's first Black woman admitted to the bar.
events.outcome: She practiced estate and family law with her husband.
events.limit: This documents her actual practice, not the hiring policies of other firms or current admission requirements.

source.title: University of Pennsylvania Archives · Sadie Tanner Mossell Alexander
source.locator: Biographical paragraphs covering employment after her doctorate and law study, bar admission and practice
source.supports: Alexander’s degree, bar admission, earlier employment difficulty and estate/family-law practice.

events.title: Charles Hamilton Houston strengthens Howard’s civil-rights training
events.people: Charles Hamilton Houston and Howard law students, including Thurgood Marshall
events.decisionMaker: Howard appointed Houston vice-dean; he directed the curriculum changes.
events.barrier: Howard had offered law courses part-time in the evening.
events.change: After his 1929 appointment, Houston developed an accredited, full-time program with stronger civil-rights instruction.
events.outcome: A 1931 memorandum documents his curriculum review. The school trained lawyers who went on to challenge racial exclusion.
events.limit: This connects an academic appointment to legal training, not every graduate’s later hiring or a reader’s present employer.

source.title: Smithsonian · Howard Law: Preparing for Struggle
source.locator: Opening paragraph and 1931 course-syllabus memorandum caption
source.supports: Houston’s appointment, curriculum changes and the dated memorandum.

events.title: William Hastie practices law inside the Interior Department
events.people: William Henry Hastie, Nathan Margold and Harold Ickes
events.decisionMaker: Hastie recalled that Secretary Ickes gave Solicitor Margold discretion to select his legal staff.
events.barrier: This opening depended on an appointment to a federal legal office, beyond obtaining a degree or bar admission.
events.change: Hastie served as assistant solicitor at the U.S. Department of the Interior.
events.outcome: His assignments included legal work on a corporate structure for the Virgin Islands’ sugar and rum industries.
events.limit: The Federal Judicial Center dates service from 1933; Hastie recalled 1934. A personnel record is needed to resolve that difference. Neither source establishes all departmental hiring practices.

source.title: Truman Library · William Hastie oral history
source.supports: Hastie’s account of selection authority, legal assignments and a 1934 start.

sources.title: Federal Judicial Center · William Henry Hastie
sources.supports: The official career chronology, which differs from his later recollection.

events.title: Jane Bolin enters New York City’s legal department
events.decisionMaker: New York City appointed Bolin assistant corporation counsel; the cited account does not name the appointing official.
events.barrier: The city identifies her as its first Black woman in this attorney role.
events.change: Bolin joined the Law Department in 1937, after private practice.
events.outcome: She represented the city in Domestic Relations Court matters before her separate judicial appointment in 1939.
events.limit: This is an attorney appointment at a named employer. It does not establish access to every city legal position or the circumstances of a present employee’s hiring.

source.title: NYC Law Department · Law Day statement
source.locator: May 1, 2020; final paragraph on Jane Bolin
source.supports: The 1937 assistant corporation counsel appointment and its institutional first.

sources.title: Historical Society of the New York Courts · Judge Jane Bolin
sources.locator: Early practice, corporation counsel and 1939 judicial appointment paragraphs
sources.supports: The transition from private practice and work before the Domestic Relations Court.

events.title: Constance Baker Motley moves from law clerk to civil-rights counsel
events.decisionMaker: The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund hired and promoted Motley.
events.barrier: Black women had little representation in the organization’s early legal staff.
events.change: She started at LDF as a law clerk in 1945 and became assistant special counsel in 1949.
events.outcome: She later led university-desegregation litigation, including the legal campaign for James Meredith’s admission to the University of Mississippi.
events.limit: This establishes a career at LDF. It does not establish employment at the NAACP, its local branches or other law firms.

source.title: Legal Defense Fund · Life and Legacy of Constance Baker Motley
source.locator: Life and Legacy biography and Desegregation Architect section
source.supports: The 1945 entry, 1949 promotion and university-desegregation work.

events.title: Heman Sweatt's challenge defeats separate law-school access
events.people: Heman Marion Sweatt and his legal team
events.decisionMaker: The U.S. Supreme Court; Chief Justice Fred Vinson delivered the opinion.
events.barrier: Texas rejected Sweatt's application because he was Black and offered a separate law school.
events.change: The Court found the separate education unequal, including its professional networks and standing, and required admission to the University of Texas Law School.
events.outcome: The judgment reversed the denial of relief and established Sweatt's right to admission.
events.limit: The opinion concerns this admission dispute; it is not evidence of degree completion, employment or equal access across all law schools.

source.title: U.S. Supreme Court · Sweatt v. Painter, 339 U.S. 629 (1950)
source.supports: The exclusion challenged, unequal education finding and required admission.

events.title: Constance Baker Motley receives a federal judicial commission
events.decisionMaker: President Lyndon B. Johnson nominated her; the U.S. Senate confirmed her.
events.barrier: The Southern District identifies her appointment as the first lifetime federal judgeship held by a Black woman.
events.change: Johnson nominated her on January 26, 1966; confirmation and her commission followed on August 30.
events.outcome: She served on the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York and became chief judge in 1982.
events.limit: A judicial appointment has a different route from an attorney, clerk or court-staff job. Her appointment does not prove the hiring history of those roles.

source.title: Federal Judicial Center · Constance Baker Motley
source.locator: Federal Judicial Service: nomination, confirmation, commission and chief-judge dates
source.supports: The appointing authorities, exact 1966 dates and 1982 leadership role.

sources.title: Southern District of New York · Court history
sources.locator: Court-history paragraph on Motley’s August 30, 1966 appointment
sources.supports: The court’s identification of the historic appointment.

furtherResearch: Find appointment letters, payrolls, staff directories and partnership records for the reader’s exact legal employer.
Follow legal credentials into actual clients and work; Ray’s business closure demonstrates why admission alone is insufficient.
Resolve the 1933/1934 discrepancy in Hastie’s Interior start date from a contemporary personnel file.
Trace law-school training, civil-rights organizations, government practice and judicial appointments as separate routes.
Identify later hiring and promotion decisions at each named institution before claiming that one appointment opened every subsequent position.
Expand public defense, prosecution, corporate counsel and private-firm practice with employer-specific records.

credential.name: Charlotte E. Ray
credential.credential: Law degree and admission to practice
credential.record: Howard records Ray's law graduation and admission to District of Columbia practice in 1872.
credential.work: DC’s Attorney General records that she opened a practice but could not sustain it because she could not attract enough business as a woman of color.

sources.supports: Law graduation and admission to District practice.
